title: Research on Cu and Sr Addition to Modified EN AW-6082-Based Alloy and Analysis of Mechanical and Electrical Properties of Obtained Materials
abstract: Abstract This study investigates Cu and Sr microalloying as two mechanistically different strategies to improve the strength-conductivity balance of a modified EN AW-6082-type Al-Mg-Si alloy for load- and current-carrying railway traction components. A Si-rich base composition (AlMg0.6Si1), selected from a prior Mg/Si optimization, was produced by metallurgical synthesis and then alloyed with Cu (0.4 wt.% and 0.6 wt.%) or Sr (0.02 wt.% and 0.05 wt.%). After casting, the materials were subjected to homogenization/solution treatment followed by artificial aging at 170–200°C for up to 24 h to map precipitation-response kinetics. Hardness and electrical conductivity were measured in the as-cast condition, after solution/homogenization, and throughout aging. The results show that Cu additions increase peak hardness but reduce conductivity, whereas Sr provides a measurable increase in hardness with a much smaller penalty in conductivity. The systematic time-temperature dataset enables a quantitative comparison between Cu and Sr modifications and identifies aging conditions that maximize the hardness-conductivity trade-off.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: In general, Al-Mg-Si alloys enable precipitation hardening due to the variable solid-state solubility of their two fundamental components, i.e., magnesium and silicon. Both of the above-mentioned elements form eutectic systems with aluminum, with a maximum content of 14.5 wt.% Mg and 12.5 wt.% Si. The precipitation hardening of these materials occurs primarily because of the separation of the Mg 2 Si phase from the solution. 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 – 5  As a result, these alloys are characterized by a high set of mechanical and electrical properties, which can ultimately be designed depending on the alloy's chemical composition, the degree and nature of the strengthening method, and the type of applied heat treatment. 6  The final properties of a given alloy depend to a large extent on the amount of alloy additions forming the Mg 2 Si phase. It is believed that increasing the magnesium and silicon content increases the alloy's strength and hardness, while reducing its plasticity and increasing its brittleness, especially under dynamic external forces. 7 ,  8 ,  9 ,  10 – 11  In addition, these materials are characterized by very high corrosion resistance, which enables their widespread use, e.g., as structural elements in transport-related industries. 12 ,  13 – 14

In this study, a new type of 6xxx series aluminum-based alloy was analyzed and developed to find a suitable construction material for a newly designed railway and tramway cantilever system dedicated to high-speed overhead lines. Based on the literature analysis and considering our own technological knowledge, we propose that the EN AW-6082 alloy will be a good base material for further study because it has high strength properties (similar to the properties of basic structural steels) and relatively good formability in the extrusion process (which was previously selected as the probable manufacturing process for cantilever individual components). Notably, this material is dedicated to highly loaded structural applications, which are important parts of the cantilever system working conditions. In addition, the EN AW-6082 alloy has a fine-grained microstructure, making it highly resistant to various types of dynamic loads. 15 ,  16 – 17

In materials and process engineering, process parameters like microstructure, material state, and exploitative properties are increasingly expected to be established systematically and quantitatively. Following the same methodological rationale, the present work applies a broad and regular artificial aging matrix to link heat-treatment conditions with hardness and electrical conductivity quantitatively. 31 , 32  The first part of this study aimed to determine the optimal Mg-Si ratio in EN AW-6082. This, in conjunction with the heat treatment conditions, will determine the type and amount of the strengthening phase and thus the level of final strength properties. The research results from the above-mentioned work were partially presented in Ref.  18 . As shown by the authors, the best mechanical properties can be achieved for alloy no. 5 with 0.4wt.% Fe, 1.1wt.% Mg, 1wt.% Si, and 0.4wt.% Mn. However, based on the additional research, done in this area, i.e., mechanical property analysis after extrusion and heat treatment, we found that alloy no. 4 (0.4wt.% Fe, 0.6wt.% Mg, 1wt.% Si, and 0.4wt.% Mn) has optimal mechanical properties, so it was selected for further research, which included the influence of additions of various alloying elements to the base alloy on the material's final mechanical properties. For the intended application, electrical conductivity must be considered along with strength. In our prior optimization study, alloy no. 4 (0.6 wt.% Mg, 1.0 wt.% Si) achieved an electrical conductivity of ~ 24 MS/m after homogenization/solution treatment while retaining moderate hardness (~61 HV5), whereas alloy no. 5 (1.1wt.% Mg, 1.2wt.% Si) exhibited higher hardness (~77 HV5) but substantially lower conductivity (~22 MS/m).

To further improve the mechanical and/or exploitation properties of the EN AW-6082 alloy, a detailed literature and experimental analysis was performed, which allowed the selection of various potential alloy additives. For railway traction components that carry both mechanical loads and electric current, alloy selection requires a quantified balance between mechanical strength and electrical conductivity. In Al-Mg-Si alloys, this balance is largely governed by the number of solute atoms retained in the α-Al matrix (which strongly reduces conductivity via electron scattering) and the precipitation state after heat treatment (strengthening by coherent precipitates while partially restoring conductivity via solute depletion). In this context, Cu and Sr were selected as two mechanistically different alloying strategies. Cu is known to increase peak-age strength in Al-Mg-Si alloys by promoting a more complex precipitation pathway involving Cu-bearing precipitates (e.g., Q′/Q-related phases) in addition to the classic β″/β′ sequence while typically decreasing electrical conductivity. In contrast, Sr exhibits extremely low solid solubility in α-Al and tends to partition into intermetallic particles; studies on 6xxx extrusion alloys report that Sr can modify the morphology of Fe-Si intermetallics (promoting α-AlFeSi over β-AlFeSi), thereby improving hot workability and potentially reducing homogenization sensitivity with only a minor loss in conductivity. 28 ,  29 – 30  Literature analysis shows that addition of approximately 0.6% copper increases the AlMgSi alloy's hardness by about 10 HV. A further increase also results in increased hardness (on average, an increase of approximately 22–25 HV for every 1%  copper addition). However, as the authors showned, achieving maximum hardness requires a longer aging time (at the same aging temperature). 19  On the other hand, the addition of Sr does not seem to affect the mechanical properties; however, it significantly affects the separation mechanism of primary Al-Fe-Si phases, promoting the formation of α- rather than β-phases. 20  As the authors state, on a macroscopic scale, this gives better hot deformability of the material and enables elimination or shortening of the homogenization process.

Compared with prior studies that typically focus on either Mg/Si optimization or single alloying additions, the novelty of the present work lies in coupling a deliberately modified Mg-Si ratio with Cu and Sr microalloying and mapping the resulting hardness-conductivity evolution over a broad aging time-temperature range. This enables a direct, application-oriented comparison of two distinct strategies (Cu-driven precipitation strengthening versus Sr-driven intermetallic modification) to improve the strength-conductivity balance.

sections.heading: Methods
paragraphs: Studies were carried out on the metallurgical synthesis, casting, and heat treatment of previously studied and optimized EN AW-6082 alloys with a narrowed range and number of individual alloy additives. As shown in Ref.   18 , changing the Mg-to-Si ratio in 6xxx-series alloys allows obtaining materials with significantly different mechanical and electrical properties. Based on the results of the research presented in Ref.   18  and following experimental works done on the subject, an alloy with the most favorable set of properties, i.e., AlMg 0.6 Si 1 , was selected and manufactured as the base material, which was additionally enriched with microadditions of copper (0.4% and 0.6%, respectively) and strontium (0.02% and 0.05%)—see Table  I . Table I Chemical composition of alloys subjected to metallurgical synthesis, casting, and heat treatment with various alloy additives Alloy Alloying elements (wt.%) Fe Mg Si Mn Ti Cu Sr Al AlMg0.6Si1 0.4 0.6 1 0.4 0.05 – – Rem AlMg0.6Si1Cu0.4 0.4 0.6 1 0.4 0.05 0.4 – Rem AlMg0.6Si1Cu0.6 0.4 0.6 1 0.4 0.05 0.6 – Rem AlMg0.6Si1Sr0.02 0.4 0.6 1 0.4 0.05 – 0.02 Rem AlMg0.6Si1Sr0.05 0.4 0.6 1 0.4 0.05 – 0.05 Rem

In the initial stage of metallurgical synthesis, EN AW-1370 aluminum was heated and melted in a resistance furnace at 750°C. The next step was the addition of master alloys and pure elements to obtain the required chemical composition in accordance with Table  I  (pure magnesium, AlSi50, AlMn12, and AlFe75 master alloys, and a structure modifier in the form of AlTi5B1 master alloy). Then, the liquid metal was thoroughly mixed and left in the furnace for another 20 min to homogenize the chemical composition. After melting and alloying, the liquid metal (AlMg0.6Si1 alloy) was poured into a graphite crucible and left to crystallize. In alloys containing 0.4, 0.6 wt. of% Cu and 0.02 and 0.05 wt.% of Sr additives, the appropriate contents of the AlCu50 and AlSr10 master alloys were added to the crucible, and the liquid metal was thoroughly mixed and left in a furnace heated to 750°C for an additional 10 min. Then, the gravity casting of each alloy in the graphite mold began. In each case, a casting (40 mm diameter and 90 mm height) was obtained.

In the first stage, the chemical composition of the castings was analyzed using a Foundry-Master Xpert OES analyzer. Samples were taken from the upper, middle, and lower parts of each casting. Each sample was subjected to five measurements, from which the average chemical composition value was taken. The collected samples were also tested for Vickers hardness, which was assessed with the a 5-kgf load and 2.5-mm-diameter carbide ball tip. On each of the castings, five measurements were made along the cross-sectional diameter. Materials in the as-cast condition were also subjected to electrical-conductivity tests by taking 10 measurements per casting and calculating the average value.

Because 6xxx-series aluminum alloys are precipitation-hardened materials, in the next step, all castings were homogenized at 550°C for 100 h and then water-quenched to supersaturate the metal. The next stage of the research procedure included artificial aging of the obtained materials in a wide temperature and time range so that it was possible to unambiguously determine the impact of both heat treatment parameters and chemical compositions of alloys on the final mechanical and electrical properties of the alloys. Therefore, each material was aged at 170, 180, 190, and 200°C for up to 24 h with 1-h intervals. At each stage of heat treatment (after homogenization and after each stage of aging), the materials were subjected to Vickers hardness and electrical conductivity analyses. The heat-treatment window (170–200°C, up to 24 h) was selected to systematically cover the under-, peak-, and over-aging regimes typically reported for 6082-type Al-Mg-Si alloys. The homogenization/solution temperature was chosen to reduce microsegregation and to dissolve Mg-Si constituents while avoiding incipient melting.

sections.heading: Results and Discussion
paragraphs: After metallurgical synthesis and gravity casting, each sample was subjected to chemical composition analysis to verify accuracy and compliance with the assumed composition. All materials had alloying additive contents similar to those previously assumed, as confirmed by the results shown in Table  II . Table II Test results of the chemical compositions of individual alloys obtained during metallurgical synthesis and gravity casting Alloy Alloying elements (wt.%) Fe Mg Si Mn Ti Cu Sr Al AlMg0.6Si1 0.36 0.55 0.97 0.4 0.052 – – Rem AlMg0.6Si1Cu0.4 0.36 0.54 1.03 0.39 0.055 0.39 – Rem AlMg0.6Si1Cu0.6 0.39 0.59 1.01 0.4 0.053 0.62 – Rem AlMg0.6Si1Sr0.02 0.42 0.52 1.01 0.42 0.051 – 0.0207 Rem AlMg0.6Si1Sr0.05 0.45 0.59 1.06 0.42 0.055 – 0.0489 Rem

In the next stage of the research, the hardness and electrical conductivity of the base alloy, i.e., AlMg0.6Si1 and alloys with following additives, 0.4 and 0.6 wt.% Cu, 0.02 and 0.05 wt.% Sr, were analyzed. All materials were then tested in both the as-cast condition and after homogenization. The measurement results are shown in Figs.  1  and  2 . The analysis of the as-cast condition shows that, from a mechanical standpoint, no significant changes in the hardness of the AlMg0.6Si1 alloy were observed as a result of the addition of copper or strontium. The base alloy had a hardness of 53.6 HV5. The addition of copper did not improve the base material's strength in the as-cast condition, and the hardness was 50.1 HV5 for the AlMg0.6Si1Cu0.4 alloy and 52.1 HV5 for the AlMg0.6Si1Cu0.6 alloy. However, a slight strengthening of the base alloy was observed when strontium was added. With a Sr content of 0.02 wt.%, samples had a hardness of 56 HV5. A further increase of Sr content up to 0.05 wt.% allowed us to obtain a hardness of 55 HV5. Regarding the electrical properties, the observed changes in the electrical conductivity of both analyzed materials were even smaller than for hardness; both materials exhibited electrical conductivity in the range of 20.2 MS/m−21.1 MS/m. Fig. 1 Mechanical and electrical properties of the tested alloys in the as-cast condition. Fig. 2 Mechanical and electrical properties of tested alloys after homogenization.

Homogenization at 550°C for 100 h changed both the mechanical and electrical properties. In the homogenized state, an increase in hardness was clearly observed for both the copper-enriched alloys (from 58.6 HV5 for the base alloy to 61.4 HV5 for 0.4 wt.% Cu and 62.6 HV5 with 0.6 wt.% Cu). Slightly higher hardness was observed for strontium: 0.02 wt.% resulted in 64.8 HV5, and 0.05 wt.% yielded 66.7 HV5. Regarding the electrical properties, a noticeable influence of the tested alloy additives on the base material's properties is observed. This is mainly seen for copper, where its addition at 0.4 wt.% decreases the electrical conductivity from 23.7 MS/m to 22.7 MS/m. Alloys with strontium additions exhibited electrical properties nearly identical to those of the base alloy, ranging from 23.7 to 23.8 MS/m. Alloys with strontium additions showed electrical properties almost identical to those of the base alloy, varying from 23.7 MS/m to 23.8 MS/m.

All samples obtained in as-cast condition were subjected to microstructural analysis using SEM; the results are presented in Fig.  3 . Fig. 3 Cumulative SEM analysis of the produced Al-Mg-Si alloys in as-cast condition.

As shown in Fig.  3 , all alloys in the as-cast condition exhibit a similar structure to the visible AlFeSi phases (both α and β)—a light-colored phase and Mg₂Si phase particles, which are seen as a dark-colored phase, consistent with the reports in the literature. 21 ,  22 ,  23 – 24  This was confirmed by EDS analyses of all samples; as an example, the initial AlMg0.6Si1 alloy is presented in Fig.  4 . Fig. 4 EDS analysis of AlMg0.6Si1 alloy in as-cast condition with visible Mg2Si, α-AlFeMnSi, and β-AlFeSi phase distributions.

The aging temperature primarily controls the precipitation kinetics: increasing the temperature accelerates solute diffusion and therefore shifts the hardening curves to shorter times (shorter time-to-peak hardness) while promoting earlier onset of over-aging (coarsening and/or transformation of strengthening precipitates). In parallel, electrical conductivity tends to increase during aging as Mg/Si (and partly Cu) atoms are removed from solid solution to precipitates, thereby reducing electron scattering. Consequently, each aging condition should be discussed not only by peak hardness but also by time to peak, conductivity at peak hardness, and the resulting hardness-conductivity trade-off.

After homogenization, each of the five alloys was subjected to an artificial aging process with a temperature range of 170°C to 200°C and time of 1 h to 24 h; therefore, materials in the T6 condition were obtained. Figures  5 – 8  show the evolution of the mechanical and electrical properties of the tested alloys during heat treatment. Aging the base AlMg0.6Si1 alloy at 170°C (Fig.  5 ) resulted in a maximum hardness of 106 HV5 and an electrical conductivity of 25.4 MS/m after 14 h. Enrichment of the base alloy with the addition of 0.4 wt.% copper allowed increasing the mechanical properties to 117 HV5. The introduction of 0.6 wt.% copper enables achieving a hardness of 122 HV5. For both alloys aged at 170°C, the maximum hardness was obtained after 19 h; their electrical conductivity was lower than that of the base alloy, about 24.1 MS/m. The addition of 0.02 wt.% and 0.05 wt.% strontium, respectively, also allowed increasing the hardness of the tested materials to 119 HV5 and 114.5 HV5, respectively (19 h of artificial aging). Importantly, the addition of strontium does not relate to a significant decrease in the electrical conductivity of AlMg0.6Si1Sr alloys (25.6 MS/m and 26 MS/m, respectively) compared with the base alloy. Fig. 5 Evolution of the mechanical and electrical properties of all tested alloys during the artificial aging process at 170°C for up to 24 h.

By increasing the aging temperature to 180°C (see Fig.  6 ), the achieve maximum mechanical properties could be achieved in less time than at 170°C. The base alloy achieved a hardness of 107.1 HV5 when aged for 12 h (the electrical conductivity of the material in this case was 26.4 MS/m). In copper-enriched alloys, the highest hardness was observed after 14 h of aging and equaled 115.7 HV5 for the AlMg0.6Si1Cu0.4 alloy and 116.7 HV5 for the AlMg0.6Si1Cu0.6 alloy. The electrical conductivity of these materials is about 2 MS/m lower than in the base metal: 24.6 MS/m (for 0.4 wt.% Cu) and 24.2 MS/m (for 0.6 wt.% Cu). For alloys with strontium addition, increased hardness compared with the base material can also be clearly seen at 114.7 HV5 and 118.7 HV5, respectively, for AlMg0.6Si1Sr0.02 and AlMg0.6Si1Sr0.05 alloys, with practically unchanged electrical conductivity (25.8 MS/m and 26.6 MS/m). Fig. 6 Evolution of the mechanical and electrical properties of all tested alloys during artificial aging at 180°C for up to 24 h.

A similar range of properties was obtained at 190°C (Fig.  7 ); the highest hardness was observed after 5 h for AlMg0.6Si1 with 0.4 and 0.6 wt.% Cu and after 4 h for strontium-enriched alloys. After this time, the following set of properties was obtained for each alloy: AlMg0.6Si1 (106.2 HV5 and 26.9 MS/m), AlMg0.6Si1Cu0.4 (115 HV5 and 24.7 MS/m), AlMg0.6Si1Cu0.6 (119 HV5 and 24.8 MS/m), AlMg0.6Si1Sr0.02 (120 HV5 and 26.2 MS/m), and AlMg0.6Si1Sr0.05 (117 HV5 and 25.4 MS/m). Based on the above, it can be concluded that the addition of 0.4 wt.% Cu allows  increasing the hardness by 8.3% compared with the hardness of the base material. For 0.6 wt.% copper amount, this increase is 12%. The addition of 0.02 wt.% and 0.05 wt.% strontium allows increasing the strength by 13 and 10.2%, respectively. Notably, at this aging temperature, for each of the alloys, a decrease in electrical properties is observed relative to the base alloy. A decrease of 2.2 MS/m−2.3 MS/m for copper addition and of 0.8 MS/m−1.6 MS/m for strontium alloy addition was observed (for an aging time guaranteeing maximum hardness).

The last temperature variant of the artificial aging process at 200°C (see Fig.  8 ) shows that for each of the tested alloys, a maximum hardness can be reached with relatively short aging times (about 2–3 h of artificial aging), followed by a decrease in the hardness of the tested materials due to their over-aging phenomena. For each of the materials, slightly lower strength properties are obtained regarding the temperatures of 170°C, 180°C, and 190°C. However, in each case, higher hardness is observed for alloys enriched with copper (111 HV5 and 117 HV5 for 0.4 wt.% Cu and 0.6 wt.% Cu) and for those with added strontium (115 HV5 and 113.7 HV5 for 0.02 wt.% Sr and 0.05 wt.% of Sr, respectively) relative to the hardness of the base AlMg0.6Si1 alloy at 105.4 HV5. Considering the electricity, the highest conductivity after 3 h of aging was shown by the base alloy (27.7 MS/m). A slight decrease in conductivity was observed when strontium was added to the alloy (to 27 MS/m at 0.02 wt.% Sr and 26 MS/m at 0.05 wt.% Sr). Like the lower aging temperatures, the highest degradation of electrical properties at 200°C was caused by introducing 0.4 wt.% and 0.6 wt.% copper (to 24.7 MS/m). Fig. 7 Evolution of the mechanical and electrical properties of all tested alloys during artificial aging at 190°C for up to 24 h. Fig. 8 Evolution of mechanical and electrical properties of all tested alloys during the artificial aging process at 200°C for up to 24 h.

The microstructural analyses of the samples after the aging process are shown in Fig.  9  (for 200°C and 3 h aging variant, which has the best electrical conductivity-to-hardness ratio). In all microstructural images, the Al-Fe-Si phase is seen; it is not completely dissolved (it is thermodynamically too stable) during the homogenization and solution heat treatment processes and is the result of structural transformations occurring in 6000-series alloys during the casting process. 23 , 24  On the presented images, small precipitates (needles and rounded/dot-like) are also visible. They are probably Fe/Mn-rich Al-Si particles and the fine dispersoids formed after homogenization. However, a thorough, detailed analysis of the SEM results did not reveal any discernible effect of either the copper alloying addition or strontium. Therefore, additional EDS examinations were conducted to determine whether these elements are present in the observed Cu and Sr precipitates (Figs.  10  and  11 ). It should be emphasized that the main strengthening entities in peak-aged Al-Mg-Si alloys (β″ needles and related clusters) are typically on the nanometer scale and cannot be reliably resolved by conventional SEM imaging. Consequently, substantial changes in hardness and electrical conductivity can occur because of nanoscale precipitation and solute redistribution, even if SEM-visible micrometer-scale constituents (Fe-rich intermetallics, larger Mg2Si particles, dispersoids) appear similar. A definitive differentiation of Cu- and Sr-related precipitation effects would therefore require nanoscale techniques such as TEM and/or DSC. Fig. 9 Cumulative results of SEM analyses of the obtained types of aluminum alloys with Cu and Sr additions after the aging process (200°C/3 h). Fig. 10 EDS analysis of AlMg0.6Si1Cu0.6 alloy after artificial aging (200°C/3 h). Fig. 11 EDS analysis of AlMg0.6Si1Sr0.05 alloy after artificial aging (200°C/3 h).

For copper addition (Fig.  10 ), EDS analysis did not detect this element in the aluminum matrix. This likely means that copper is either in solid solution and has not formed detectable precipitates or the copper-containing precipitates (e.g., Q′/Q, Al₅Cu₂Mg₈Si₆, or θ, Al₂Cu) are too small to see using the applied SEM technique.

In general, in the 6082 alloy, the addition of copper up to ~ 1 wt.% primarily dissolves into the α-Al matrix during proper solution treatment, possibly forming early solute clustering/GP zones and subsequently partitioning into Cu-bearing precipitates during aging. Specifically, it modifies the classic β′′/β′ (Mg 2 Si) sequence by promoting the formation of metastable Q′ and stable Q (Al₅Cu₂Mg₈Si₆) phases—sometimes accompanied by θ (Al₂Cu) if it is retained from casting (as in the samples described in this article) or incompletely dissolved after homogenization, thereby accelerating the precipitation kinetics and increasing peak hardness/strength. 25 , 26
In contrast to the Cu-containing alloy, EDS analysis of the strontium-modified alloy clearly confirmed the presence of strontium within the primary Al-Fe-Si precipitates (Fig.  11 ).

According to the literature, 20 , 27  in the 6082-type alloy, strontium exhibits extremely low solid solubility in α-Al and therefore partitions predominantly into intermetallic particles rather than remaining in solid solution. Specifically, Sr forms Sr-bearing phases such as Al₄Sr and Al₂Si₂Sr (or their nanometer-scale precursors) and is frequently detected within primary Fe-containing intermetallics (Al-Fe-Si-Mn), where it alters the phase selection and morphology of Fe-bearing particles (favoring α-AlFeSi over β-AlFeSi) during solidification. At typical modification levels (ppm to hundreds of ppm), Sr strongly interacts with Si, while at higher additions (approaching wt.%), precipitation of Al₂Si₂Sr becomes probable already during solidification; consequently, SEM/EDS commonly reveals Sr associated with primary Al-Fe-Si-(Mn) particles, whereas its presence in the α-Al matrix at room temperature is expected to be negligible apart from possible trace-level solute or nanoscale Al-Si-Sr clusters below SEM detectability.

Hardness and electrical conductivity provide a practical, sensitive screening of precipitation response and the strength-conductivity trade-off. Nevertheless, they do not fully represent the mechanical performance under service loads. Therefore, for application-level qualification of traction components, tensile properties (YS/UTS/elongation) and, depending on the duty cycle, fatigue and corrosion-related performance should be assessed for selected peak-aged conditions.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Based on the conducted research, 6xxx-series alloys with increased strength can be obtained by alloying them with copper and strontium. Differences in both mechanical and electrical properties are not significantly visible in the as-cast condition. For the homogenized material, a tendency emerges indicating that the addition of both copper and strontium strengthens the AlMg0.6Si1 alloy, whereas strontium does not adversely affect the electrical properties, and copper decreases the electrical conductivity of the tested material. During heat treatment of the tested group of alloys in the temperature range of 170–200°C and time of 1–24 h, the base alloy in the tested temperature range obtains its maximum hardness in the range of 105.4–107 HV5. The addition of 0.4 wt.% copper increased the hardness to 111–117 HV5. The AlMg0.6Si1Cu0.6 alloy exhibits slightly higher mechanical properties, which range from 116.7 HV5 to 122 HV5. However, copper significantly degrades the electrical properties of the base alloy by as much as 2.5–3 MS/m. An addition of 0.02 wt.% strontium increased the hardness of the base alloy during heat treatment by 11–15 HV5 (depending on aging temperature and time), with practically unchanged electrical conductivity (a decrease of at most 0.6 MS/m). Adding 0.05 wt.% strontium increased hardness by about 8–13 HV5, while the decrease in electrical conductivity was up to 1.8 MS/m (conductivity increased with increasing aging temperature). Based on the conducted tests, both copper and strontium allow increasing the mechanical properties of 6XXX alloys. However, the introduction of copper significantly affects the deterioration of their electrical properties, and the addition of strontium has a negligible effect on the electrical conductivity of the tested materials.
